ambition.rationale:
The core problem is an inverse problem, not a familiar app with a model attached. The repo back-traces a fire's ignition location, start time and spread-rate scale from sparse timed perimeters (s11_ignition.py:192), calibrates the 90% uncertainty per fire on synthetic cases (s11:9, s11:439), and withholds the start time when the data do not pin it down (s11:299). Both real fires come back not identifiable (README.md:134), which shows the problem is hard and left open, not solved. The LLM analyst is peripheral and not run live (README.md:53, web/api/analyst.ts:47), so it earns no credit here.

The methods are not new. The forward model is classical Rothermel/Anderson-style spread with Dijkstra travel times (spread.py:3, spread.py:12, spread.py:194), so the hardness sits in the inversion and calibration discipline, not in invented physics.

Recency is split by half, as the rubric asks. The debris-flow half (Risk tab) meets the "not possible a year ago" test in part. It trains and scores on a 2026-titled USGS inventory: 7,639 records from 77 fires in leave-one-fire-out CV (model_eval.json; s14_debris_models.py:77). The ScienceBase ID prefix decodes to 2026-01-09, which corroborates the 2026 date but is an inference from the ID format. Those models are ordinary (RF, MLP, refitted M1), and the repo itself says ML did not clearly beat M1 (README.md:179), so the recency credit is real but modest. The ignition half does not meet the test. Its inputs (NIFC 2025 perimeters at s05_perimeters.py:72, DINS, AVIRIS-3) were public in 2025, so they earn hardness credit only. The README's "only recently became public" (README.md:34) overreaches for those inputs.

Score 7 (weighted 17.5 before the harness arithmetic). It is clearly above an ordinary entry, but not 8: the recency-qualifying work is a tab rather than the headline, the forward physics is classical, and the one model-native piece (the Muse Spark analyst) is unrun.

depth.rationale: The hard part is real, original and mostly correct: a numba time-dependent Dijkstra over an elliptical rate-of-spread model, a hinge-loss inversion over ignition cell, start time, spread scale and shape cap, split-half simulation-based calibration of the posterior temperature, an identifiability gate, a perturbed synthetic benchmark, and hand-coded Robins-Breslow-Greenland and cluster-bootstrap statistics. The formulas I checked are right: the Anderson length-to-breadth curve, the rear-focus ellipse, the RBG variance and the Wilson interval. It stops short of 8 because the physics constants are unsourced (spread.py:57-77); the deployed Eaton fit has lb_max 1.0, which collapses the ellipse to a circle; the Palisades hold-out predicts zero burned cells at both held-out perimeters; the synthetic truth uses the same spread function; the debris models are stock scikit-learn; and the analyst is a standard tool loop with a heuristic verifier. Share estimate: whole-file upper bound of about 3,700 original-logic lines (spread.py, s11, s14, s05, debris.py, s09b, s06, s10, verify.ts) out of about 16,700 code lines (pipeline 6,739, api 1,392, web/src about 8,600), so about 22% of all code and about half the Python pipeline. Discounting report prose inside s11 and s14, the core is nearer 2,500 to 3,000 lines (about 15-18%). The rest is fetch, parsing, rendering and plumbing. Stub steps s09c, s12, s12c and s13 are not credited.

evidence.rationale: Nearly every quantitative README claim reproduces from committed files. The synthetic medians and p90s were recomputed from the 30 cases per fire, and the headline table, debris table, exposure odds ratios, weather correlations, wind ablation, and data counts all match. The debris evaluation is strong: leave-one-fire-out over 77 folds, paired bootstrap intervals, a fold-isolation test, and an honest "did not clearly beat M1" result. Negative results are reported (Eaton hold-out misses CAL FIRE's point, start times withheld, analyst eval not run). Evidence strength is uneven. Real-outcome checks are the debris LOFO, the exposure counts and the wind-station correlations. The back-trace claims rest on synthetic truth that uses the same spread equations, and on two real fires. The Palisades 315 m location win comes from a fit that predicts zero burned cells at the held-out times. The real hold-out keeps the held-out burn area inside its first fitted footprint, which RESULTS.md calls a sliver. The random forest's weak agreement with USGS is not reported, and the debris table sits outside the drift test. Score 7.5 rather than 8 because the lead feature's real validation is thin and two of its real-data claims are overstated.
